edition.copy_text: Koetschau, GCS 2–3 (1899), via the Perseus TEI

source_text: Ἴδωμεν δὲ καὶ τὴν ἑξῆς τοῦ Κέλσου λέξιν, οὕτως ἔχουσαν· Ἰουδαῖοι μὲν οὖν ἔθνος ἴδιον γενόμενοι καὶ κατὰ τὸ ἐπιχώριον νόμους θέμενοι καὶ τούτους ἐν σφίσιν ἔτι νῦν περιστέλλοντες καὶ θρησκείαν ὁποίαν δὴ, πάτριον δ᾿ οὖν, φυλάσσοντες ὅμοια τοῖς ἄλλοις ἀνθρώποις δρῶσιν, ὅτι ἕκαστοι τὰ πάτρια, ὁποῖά ποτ᾿ ἂν τύχῃ (καθεστηκότα) , περιέπουσι. δοκεῖ δ᾿ οὕτως καὶ συμφέρειν, οὐ μόνον καθότι ἐπὶ νοῦν ἦλθεν ἄλλοις ἄλλως νομίσαι καὶ δεῖ φυλάττειν τὰ ἐς κοινὸν κεκυρωμένα, ἀλλὰ καὶ ὅτι ὡς εἰκὸς τὰ μέρη τῆς γῆς ἐξ ἀρχῆς ἄλλα ἄλλοις ἐπόπταις νενεμημένα καὶ κατά τινας ἐπικρατείας διειλημμένα ταύτῃ καὶ διοικεῖται. καὶ δὴ τὰ παρ᾿ ἑκάστοις ὀρθῶς ἂν πράττοιτο ταύτῃ δρώμενα, ὅπῃ ἐκείνοις φίλον· παραλύειν δὲ οὐχ ὅσιον εἶναι τὰ ἐξ ἀρχῆς κατὰ τόπους νενομισμένα. ἐν τούτοις δὴ ὁ Κέλσος ἐμφαίνει ὅτι οἱ πάλαι Αἰγύπτιοι Ἰουδαῖοι ὕστερον ἔθνος ἐγίνοντο ἴδιον, καὶ νόμους θέμενοι τούτους περιστέλλουσι. καὶ ἵνα μὴ ἐπαναλάβωμεν τὰς ἐκκειμένας τοῦ Κέλσου λέξεις, φησὶ καὶ συμφέρειν τούτοις τὰ πάτρια θρησκεύειν ὁμοίως τοῖς ἄλλοις ἔθνεσι τὰ ἴδια περιέπουσι. καὶ βαθυτέραν τινὰ ἐκτίθεται περὶ τοῦ συμφέρειν Ἰουδαίοις περιέπειν τὰ πάτρια αἰτίαν, αἰνισσόμενος ὅτι τοὺς ἑκάστων νόμους οἱ λαχόντες ἐπόπται εἶναι τῆς γῆς τῶν νομοθετουμένων συνεργοῦντες τοῖς νομοθέταις ἔθεντο. ἔοικεν οὖν δηλοῦν ὅτι καὶ τὴν Ἰουδαίων χώραν καὶ τὸ ἐπ᾿ αὐτῆς ἔθνος ἐποπτεύει τις ἤ τινες, ὑφ᾿ οὗ ἢ ὑφ᾿ ὧν οἱ Ἰουδαίων νόμοι συνεργοῦντος ἢ συνεργούντων Μωϋσεῖ ἐτέθησαν.
thought_title: Celsus on the ancestral laws of the Jews
pass_a_gloss: Let us see (ἴδωμεν) also the next passage (λέξις) of Celsus, which runs thus: 'The Jews, then, having become a nation of their own (ἔθνος ἴδιον) and having laid down laws (νόμους θέμενοι) according to the local (ἐπιχώριον) and still now maintaining (περιστέλλοντες) these among themselves, and guarding (φυλάσσοντες) a worship (θρησκεία) of whatever sort (ὁποίαν δή), but at any rate ancestral (πάτριον), act like the other men, because each honour (περιέπουσι) their ancestral things, of whatever sort they happen to be (established). It seems thus also to be advantageous (συμφέρειν), not only inasmuch as it came to mind (ἐπὶ νοῦν ἦλθεν) to different people to think (νομίσαι) differently and one must guard what has been ratified for the common (τὰ ἐς κοινὸν κεκυρωμένα), but also because, as is likely (ὡς εἰκός), the parts of the earth from the beginning were allotted (νενεμημένα) to different overseers (ἐπόπταις) and divided (διειλημμένα) according to certain dominions (ἐπικρατείας) are also administered (διοικεῖται) in this way. And indeed the things done among each would be done rightly (ὀρθῶς) being done in this way, as is dear (φίλον) to them; and it is not holy (οὐχ ὅσιον) to dissolve/abolish (παραλύειν) what has been customary (νενομισμένα) from the beginning by places (κατὰ τόπους).' In these, Celsus indicates (ἐμφαίνει) that those of old Egyptians later became Jews, a nation of their own, and having laid down laws maintain them. And so that we may not repeat (ἐπαναλάβωμεν) Celsus's words set out (ἐκκειμένας), he says also that it is advantageous for these to worship (θρησκεύειν) their ancestral things like the other nations that honour their own. And he sets out a deeper (βαθυτέραν) cause (αἰτία) about its being advantageous for Jews to honour the ancestral things, hinting (αἰνισσόμενος) that those who obtained by lot (λαχόντες) to be overseers of the earth laid down the laws of each, working together (συνεργοῦντες) with the lawgivers (νομοθέταις) of those being given laws (τῶν νομοθετουμένων). He seems then to show that the land (χώρα) of the Jews and the nation upon it someone or some oversee (ἐποπτεύει), by whom—one or several working together with Moses—the laws of the Jews were laid down.

choices.why: οἱ πάλαι Αἰγύπτιοι Ἰουδαῖοι: 'those who were Egyptians of old later became the Jews' corrected to 'the Jews, who were Egyptians of old, later became a nation of their own'
choices.english: the Jews, who were Egyptians of old, later became a nation of their own

choices.why: ὑφ᾿ οὗ ἢ ὑφ᾿ ὧν: agency restored, 'laid down by that one or those several, working together with Moses'
τῆς γῆς τῶν νομοθετουμένων taken together by word order ('the land of the peoples receiving laws'); note records the alternative
τὰ ἐς κοινὸν κεκυρωμένα: 'ratified for the common good' changed to 'publicly ratified'
νενεμημένα ... διειλημμένα ... διοικεῖται: participle structure restored ('allotted ... and, being divided into certain dominions, are administered')
καθεστηκότα supplement now translated ('however they happen to have been established'); δοκεῖ δ᾿ οὕτως καὶ συμφέρειν 'to do so seems to be of benefit too'

pass_b_english: Let us look also at Celsus’s next passage, which runs as follows: “Now the Jews, having become a nation of their own and having laid down laws according to their local custom, still maintain them among themselves to this day; and in keeping a form of worship, whatever kind it may be, but at any rate ancestral, they act like the rest of mankind, since each people honours its ancestral customs, however they happen to have been established. And to do so seems to be of benefit too, not only because different people have come to think in different ways, and what has been publicly ratified must be preserved, but also because, as is likely, the parts of the earth were allotted from the beginning to different overseers and, being divided into certain dominions, are administered in this way. And indeed what is done among each people would be done rightly when it is done in the way that pleases them; and it is not holy to abolish the customs established in each place from the beginning.”

In these words Celsus implies that the Jews, who were Egyptians of old, later became a nation of their own, and that having laid down laws they maintain them. And, so as not to repeat Celsus’s words set out above, he says that it benefits them to practise their ancestral worship, like the other nations who honour their own customs. He also sets out a deeper cause why it benefits the Jews to honour their ancestral customs, hinting that those who were allotted to be overseers of the land of the peoples receiving laws laid down each people’s laws, working together with the lawgivers. He seems, then, to show that the land of the Jews too, and the nation living in it, is overseen by someone, or by several, and that the laws of the Jews were laid down by that one or those several, working together with Moses.
notes: Quotation from Celsus set in double quotation marks. καθεστηκότα is Koetschau's supplement, translated as 'however they happen to have been established'. τὰ ἐς κοινὸν κεκυρωμένα rendered 'what has been publicly ratified' (not 'for the common good', which adds a notion). ὅπῃ ἐκείνοις φίλον: 'them' is ambiguous in Celsus (the peoples or the overseers); left ambiguous here, since Origen reads it of the overseers at 5.27. οὐχ ὅσιον rendered 'not holy' throughout 5.25-28 to keep the ὅσιον/ἀνόσιον (holy/unholy) contrast Origen builds on; εὐσέβεια is kept as 'piety'. ἐπόπται rendered 'overseers'. The claim that the Jews were Egyptians refers back to Celsus at 3.5. τῶν νομοθετουμένων stands directly after τῆς γῆς and is taken with it ('the land of the peoples receiving laws'); it could instead go with τοῖς νομοθέταις ('the lawgivers of those receiving laws'), with no real change of sense. No Scripture quoted.

Open doubt (review): 5.25: τῶν νομοθετουμένων could go with τῆς γῆς ('the land of the peoples receiving laws') or with τοῖς νομοθέταις ('the lawgivers of those receiving laws'). The translation follows the word order and takes the first reading. The note records the alternative. The sense hardly changes.
